module.name: EU AI Act
module.purpose: Keep a register of your AI systems, classify each one under Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, and track the duties that follow from its class and your role.
module.whoNeeds: Organisations that build, sell or use AI systems in the EU, such as credit scoring, insurance pricing, CV screening or a customer chatbot.
module.whoDoesnt: Organisations with no AI systems on the EU market and no AI in use in the EU.
module.switchHint: On adds “EU AI Act” to the navigation for everyone who may read it.
module.turnedOn: The EU AI Act module is on. You'll find it in the navigation.
module.turnedOff: The EU AI Act module is off. Its data is kept.
module.open: Open the EU AI Act module

confirm.title: Turn off the EU AI Act module?
confirm.body: The module disappears for everyone, and its pages can't be opened.
confirm.kept: Nothing is deleted. The AI systems, their classifications, obligations and notes are kept, and come back unchanged when you turn the module on again.

errors.forbidden: You can't change modules. Ask an administrator.
errors.unavailable: The module couldn't be changed. Please try again in a moment.

overview.title: AI systems
overview.intro: Every AI system your organisation builds, sells or uses, its class under the EU AI Act, and what is still to do.
overview.frameworkHint: The EU AI Act isn't one of your frameworks yet. Add it in Setup → Frameworks to see its requirements in your Statement of Applicability.
overview.frameworkHintAsk: The EU AI Act isn't one of your frameworks yet. Ask an administrator to add it in Setup → Frameworks, so its requirements show in your Statement of Applicability.

empty.title: No AI systems yet
empty.body: Start with the AI you already use: a scoring engine, a chatbot, a tool that screens CVs. Add each one, answer a few questions, and you'll see which duties apply.
empty.ask: Someone who manages AI systems (the security lead or a risk owner) can add them.

form.newIntro: Describe the system in plain words. You'll classify it next.
form.editIntro: Changing your role updates which obligations apply.
form.name: Name
form.nameHint: What people call the system, such as “Credit scoring engine”.
form.descriptionHint: Optional. What it does and who uses it.
form.intendedPurposeHint: What the system is meant to be used for (Art. 3(12)), as the supplier or your own team describes it.
form.roleHint: Provider if you build it or put your name on it; deployer if you use it under your authority.
form.supplierHint: Optional. Who makes it, if not you.
form.modelHint: Optional. For example “vendor scoring engine v4”.
form.usesGpai: It is built on a general-purpose AI model
form.usesGpaiHint: For example a large language model. Recorded for context only.
form.ownerHint: The person accountable for this system.

isAiSystem.question: Is it an AI system?
isAiSystem.help: Under Art. 3(1), an AI system is machine-based and infers from its input how to produce outputs such as predictions, recommendations, content or decisions. Fixed rules written by people, like a spreadsheet formula, are not AI systems.
isAiSystem.yes: It learns from data or infers its outputs, for example a trained model or a language model.
isAiSystem.no: It only follows fixed rules people wrote. The Regulation doesn't apply.

prohibited.question: Does it do any of these?
prohibited.help: Art. 5 bans these practices outright. Leave everything unticked if none applies, which is the usual case.

annexI.question: Is it a safety component of a regulated product?
annexI.help: Art. 6(1): the system is a safety part of, or is itself, a product under the EU product laws in Annex I, such as machinery, medical devices, toys, lifts or vehicles, and that product needs a third-party conformity check.
annexI.yes: Yes, it is part of such a product, or is one.
annexI.no: No. Software used in offices, banks or insurers is usually not.

annexIII.question: Is it used for any of these?
annexIII.help: Annex III lists the uses that make a system high-risk. Tick each that applies; leave all unticked if none does.

profilesPeople.question: Does it profile people?
profilesPeople.help: Profiling means evaluating people automatically from their personal data, for example to predict their behaviour, reliability or finances (GDPR Art. 4(4)). A system that profiles is always high-risk.
profilesPeople.yes: Yes, it evaluates or predicts things about individual people.
profilesPeople.no: No, it doesn't evaluate individual people.

derogation.question: Does one of these describe its job?
derogation.help: Art. 6(3): a system listed in Annex III is not high-risk when it doesn't materially influence decisions and one of these is true. If none fits, choose “None of these”.

transparency.question: Which of these apply?
transparency.help: Art. 50 asks for openness where people could be misled. Tick each that applies, or none.
